authorKnowledgeAtRecordTime: E2-V1 generation and N1-on-A0 results were already known when E2-V2 was authored.
The old Pass-B epistemic/detection framing defect and its not_remembered pattern were already known.
differencesFromE2V1: Household composition changes from one caregiver plus grandparent and younger sibling to two caregivers plus an older cousin.
Daily mobility changes from tram/bicycle emphasis to bus/walking with occasional rides from relatives.
The public-space mix changes from community workshop, tram loop and river fields to branch library/civic hall, bus-market interchange and canalside park.
The bilingual context changes from English/Arabic to English/Tagalog.
The calendar shifts later while preserving the same ordinary childhood-through-adolescence age span and urban public-institution access pattern.
worldAuthoringRecord.reasonForDifferences: Create a second ordinary, source-free developmental substrate that is materially distinct from E2-V1 while preserving comparable access constraints. The changes were not selected to target any known remembered/not_remembered episode, desired adult identity, target personality, genome signal, or N2 score.
worldAuthoringRecord.knownConfoundDisclosure: The author could not unsee E2-V1 or the failed N1-on-A0 run. This record makes that author-after-observation fact explicit; N2 therefore remains development evidence rather than an independent population sample.

episodes.observableAction: Late on a Saturday morning, caregiver_b sits with the subject at the narrow kitchen table, where a half-finished worksheet from school is spread out beside a mug of tea and a small pile of grocery receipts. The worksheet has simple addition problems and a space at the bottom for a parent signature. Caregiver_b glances at the clock, then pulls the worksheet closer, quickly fills in the last three unanswered sums, and signs the bottom line with their name. The subject, who has been slowly working on one of the problems with a pencil, watches as caregiver_b writes, then sets the pencil down. Caregiver_b taps the page once, says that it is done now, and slides the worksheet onto the top of the subject’s school folder, which is already packed for Monday and leaning against the table leg. The subject nods and pushes their chair back while caregiver_b gathers the receipts into a stack and reaches for a shopping list pad.

On a cool Saturday morning, caregiver_b stands in the narrow kitchen, holding an open grocery bag and checking items against a handwritten list on the table. They pause, frown at the list, and say they cannot find the small coin purse they use for bus fare. The subject, who has been sitting at the table drawing on scrap paper, looks up as caregiver_b starts patting their jacket pockets and opening a few drawers. Caregiver_b asks the subject if they remember seeing the coin purse and suggests checking around the table and near the rear door. The subject slides off the chair and looks under the table, then along the floor by a pair of shoes and a folded shopping cart. After a moment, the subject spots the coin purse half-hidden under the edge of a newspaper on a chair by the rear stair door, picks it up, and holds it out. Caregiver_b turns, sees it in the subject’s hand, and steps over to take it, saying that now they can catch the bus on time. They drop the coin purse into their bag, fold the list, and tell the subject they will be back before lunch as they reach for their keys.

On a late Sunday afternoon, caregiver_a sits sideways at the narrow kitchen table with a paperback storybook open between themselves and the subject. A half-folded dish towel and an empty mug sit pushed to one side. Caregiver_a reads a paragraph aloud in English about a child taking a long train ride to visit grandparents, then pauses to turn the page. As they do, the subject points at a small illustration of a train window and asks why the picture shows trees going past if the train is supposed to be going very fast. Caregiver_a stops, looks at the picture, and leans closer, resting one elbow on the table. They trace a finger along the drawn trees and the side of the train, then glance toward the subject and say that even fast trains pass trees one by one. The subject shifts in their chair, looks from the picture to the words on the page, and keeps their finger on the window in the drawing. After a brief silence, caregiver_a clears their throat, straightens the book so it faces them again, and resumes reading the next sentence from the story.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: children's storybook about a train trip

episodes.observableAction: On a drizzly Saturday afternoon, caregiver_b and the subject enter the branch library, return a small stack of books, walk to the children’s shelves, and caregiver_b tells the subject they may choose one book while caregiver_b looks for a bus timetable, gesturing to nearby shelves and reminding the subject to avoid torn books; the subject runs a hand along the spines, tilts a few out, selects a brightly colored paperback with a rocket and planet on the cover, briefly inspects another book with a cartoon dog before replacing it, then carries the rocket book toward the front desk, where caregiver_b, now holding a folded bus leaflet, meets them, glances at the cover, nods, and says they should check it out so they can catch the next bus, after which the librarian scans caregiver_b’s card and the book’s barcode, and the subject folds the due-date slip into the front cover and holds the book while following caregiver_b toward the exit.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: children’s paperback about rockets and planets

episodes.observableAction: Late on a Saturday morning, caregiver_b and the subject step off a city bus at the municipal interchange, walk toward the indoor produce market, and near the entrance caregiver_b stops by a bench, pulls a folded shopping list and some bills from a pocket, and tells the subject to go alone to the ticket kiosk to load enough credit for two rides onto their bus card while caregiver_b goes inside to buy vegetables, pointing toward the row of kiosks, repeating the amount, and handing over the card and money before walking into the market; the subject nods, walks across the paved area to an unoccupied kiosk, stands on the worn yellow line, reads the printed instructions beside the screen, inserts the card into the slot, feeds the bills into the machine one by one, waits for the beep and the new balance on the screen, presses the button to finish, waits for the card to eject, checks the printed receipt, then returns to the bench, gives caregiver_b the card and receipt, and watches as caregiver_b glances at the balance, folds the receipt into a wallet, shifts the shopping bag, and suggests checking the time on the overhead bus schedule board.

At the municipal bus interchange beside the indoor market, caregiver_b hands the subject a note and money, instructs them to go alone to the pharmacy inside to buy a specific small bottle of generic pain tablets and a roll of adhesive bandage, and points out the shop location before walking toward the produce section while the subject follows signs to the pharmacy, waits in line, reads the note to the clerk, compares two offered tablet bottles to the written brand name, selects the exact match, requests the listed bandage width, pays, keeps the receipt, returns to caregiver_b near the bus schedule board, and gives them the pharmacy bag and remaining coins while caregiver_b checks the tablet label against the note and puts the receipt away.

On a breezy Saturday afternoon at the canalside park, the subject and their older cousin walk toward the basketball courts with plastic water bottles, pause at a low metal fence displaying poster boards, step closer to read a black-and-white photograph of the canal during a past flood, compare the image to the currently low water in the real canal behind them, then, after the cousin checks their watch and suggests moving on, the subject drops their hand from the poster and follows the cousin down the path toward the courts.

Late on a Saturday morning at the branch library, the subject walks alone past a row of public computers toward the shelves near the newspapers, pauses at a freestanding display with several thin paperbacks and stapled booklets, and scans the titles. They pick up a brightly printed booklet about local bus routes, flip through a few pages showing maps and fare tables, then set it back in the rack. Next they pull out a plain-covered paperback with small text about budgeting and bills, glance at a page with a sample monthly expense chart, and return it to the shelf. After a moment, the subject reaches for a different paperback with a bold title about saving money as a student, reads the back cover, opens to a section with headings about part-time work and transport costs, and stands reading for a short while. They then tuck this book under one arm, leave the other items on the display, and walk toward the front desk, where a short line has formed for checkouts.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: paperback guide on saving money as a student

episodes.observableAction: On a quiet Saturday morning at the branch library, the subject walks alone to the non-fiction shelves labeled philosophy and religion, briefly examines several books on world religions, ethics, and questions of meaning and belief, then selects one paperback, carries it to an empty study table, sits down, and begins reading a chapter from the beginning.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: introductory paperback on questions of meaning and belief

episodes.observableAction: On a warm Saturday afternoon at the branch library, the subject walks alone to the non-fiction shelves labeled philosophy and religion, scans the spines, and pulls out a thin paperback with a plain cover that reads "Introduction to Ethics: Questions About Right and Wrong." They carry the book to an empty study table near the back wall, sit down, and open to a chapter titled "Why Be Moral?" On the first page of the chapter, they pause over a paragraph that states that some people say actions are right because they follow rules given by a religion, while others say actions are right because they lead to the best overall consequences for everyone affected. The subject reads the paragraph slowly, then traces one sentence with a finger, looks briefly toward the nearby shelves, and returns their eyes to the page. After a few minutes, they turn the book slightly, continue reading down the page, and then flip ahead to scan the next section headings before closing the book around a finger to hold their place.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: "Introduction to Ethics: Questions About Right and Wrong" chapter "Why Be Moral?"

episodes.observableAction: Late on a Saturday morning, the subject sits at the narrow kitchen table with an open school worksheet, a pencil, and a half-finished row of simple subtraction problems. Caregiver B moves between the stove and the sink, glancing over each time they pass. After watching the subject erase and rewrite the same answer twice, Caregiver B wipes their hands on a towel, comes to the table, pulls the worksheet closer, and says they will "just finish these" so it will be done before lunch. Without asking the subject anything further, Caregiver B takes the pencil from beside the subject’s hand and quickly fills in the remaining answers, then signs the bottom of the page where the teacher has left a line for a parent signature. The subject stays seated, hands in their lap, while Caregiver B stacks the completed worksheet with a reading log on the corner of the table and tells the subject to put the papers straight into their school bag. Caregiver B then returns to stirring a pot on the stove while the subject slides off the chair and carries the small stack of papers toward the bedroom where their bag is kept.

On a mid-morning weekend, the subject sits at the narrow kitchen table with an open exercise book and a page of word problems, several questions already answered in uneven handwriting and the next one half-copied, while Caregiver B stands at the counter sorting a small pile of bills and a bus pass, glancing over each time they turn a page, then comes to stand beside the chair, slides the worksheet closer, reads the next two problems aloud in a quick, matter-of-fact tone, says there is no time to be stuck because they have to leave for a shift soon, pulls the exercise book in front of themselves, takes the pencil, writes the answers directly into the subject’s book down the page, adds the date at the top, closes the book, places it on top of the subject’s schoolbag by the kitchen doorway with a brief reminder to put it straight into the bag, and then picks up the bus pass and returns to the counter to finish sorting the bills while the subject remains seated at the table watching.

On a late afternoon, the subject sits at the narrow kitchen table with a sheet of math homework showing a column of three-digit addition problems, a few already answered in the subject’s uneven writing and the next one partly worked out with small pencil marks in the margin. Caregiver B comes in from the rear stair carrying a shopping bag, sets it on the counter, glances at the page as they pass, and asks if the homework is still not finished. Without waiting for a reply, Caregiver B pulls out a chair, sits down, turns the worksheet so it faces them, and says they need it done before they start dinner. They take the pencil from beside the subject’s hand, quickly write answers for the remaining problems down the sheet, and draw a short line under the last one. Caregiver B then signs their name at the bottom where the teacher has left space, pushes the paper back toward the subject with a brief instruction to put it straight into the schoolbag, stands up, and returns to unpacking vegetables from the shopping bag at the counter while the subject gathers the worksheet and walks toward the bedroom where the bag is kept.

On a cool Saturday morning, the subject sits at the kitchen table with a partly completed math worksheet when Caregiver B enters with a small bag of groceries, briefly looks at the page, sits beside the subject, turns the worksheet, states they need the homework finished before starting laundry, takes the pencil, quickly writes answers for all remaining problems while checking an example on the previous page, adds the last answer, draws a short line under it, signs their name at the bottom, pushes the completed work back toward the subject, tells them to put it straight into the schoolbag, then stands and unpacks groceries while the subject stacks the papers and walks toward the bedroom where the bag is kept.

On a late Saturday morning, the subject sits at the kitchen table with a math workbook of mixed multiplication and division problems, several answers already written, while a folded school test notice lies beside it as Caregiver B enters with a laundry basket, asks if the homework is still unfinished, sits next to the subject, turns the workbook, states it must be completed before hanging the washing, then quickly writes answers for the remaining problems, checks one against an example in the margin, draws a line under the last solution, signs their name on the line at the bottom of the page, closes the workbook, places it on the subject’s schoolbag by the doorway, and carries the laundry basket toward the rear stair as the subject stands and moves the schoolbag closer to the door.

Late on a Saturday morning, Caregiver B and the subject stand near the bus station ticket kiosks with two reusable shopping bags as Caregiver B hands the subject a short list and some money, instructs them to go alone into the indoor produce market to buy onions, tomatoes, and rice, and stay to check bus times while the subject walks through the sliding doors, compares prices at two vegetable stalls, asks for the listed amounts, waits while the vegetables are weighed, pays and checks the change and receipt, then goes to a grain counter to read the rice prices, request the listed amount, pay, and pocket the second receipt and remaining coins before carrying the filled bags back outside to the bus area, where they approach Caregiver B, show the purchases, and hand over the receipts and change.

At the bus interchange beside the indoor market, Caregiver B gives the subject a shopping list, money, and a coin purse, indicates the market and bus timetables, says they will meet back in about forty minutes, and leaves while the subject goes alone into the market to buy the listed vegetables, rice, soap, and cooking oil, comparing prices, checking labels, paying and keeping receipts, then checks the bus timetable for the next day’s first-morning departure time, returns to the meeting spot with two filled reusable bags, shows Caregiver B the purchases, receipts, and remaining coins, points out the correct bus time on the timetable, and then walks with Caregiver B toward the bus queue carrying one bag each.

On a quiet Saturday afternoon at the branch library, the subject stands in front of a low shelf marked "Philosophy / Religion" with several thin paperbacks and thicker hardcovers lined up together. After scanning the spines, they pull out two different books, one titled "World Religions: An Introduction" and another with a darker cover titled "Questions of Right and Wrong," flip through a few pages of each while standing in the aisle, then slide the first book back into its place and carry the second to a nearby study table. Sitting down, they open to the first chapter, read a page that sets out a short list of statements beginning with "Some people say that what is right depends only on what a society accepts," pause to look back at the chapter heading, then continue reading down the page for several minutes before closing the book briefly to check the title again and then reopening it to the same spot.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: "Questions of Right and Wrong" introductory ethics book

episodes.observableAction: On a mid-afternoon in early March, the subject walks into the branch library, signs their name on the small clipboard at the front desk for computer use, and then moves past the public terminals toward the shelves. They stop again at the section marked "Philosophy / Religion," scan the spines, and pull out the same dark-covered book titled "Questions of Right and Wrong" along with a different paperback titled "Everyday Ethics: Stories and Dilemmas." Standing in the aisle, they flip through a few pages of the second book, glance at a page heading that reads "Telling the Truth and Telling Lies," then close it halfway and look back at the first book’s table of contents. After a short pause, they slide "Everyday Ethics" back into its place, keep "Questions of Right and Wrong" in hand, and carry it to an empty study table near the notice board. Sitting down, they open to a later chapter where a bolded sentence near the top of the page reads, "Some philosophers argue that an action can be wrong even if everyone approves of it," run a finger under that line, and then continue reading down the page for several minutes without taking out any notebook or other materials.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: "Questions of Right and Wrong" ethics book

episodes.observableAction: On a late Sunday afternoon, the subject sits alone at a study table in the branch library with the dark-covered book "Questions of Right and Wrong" open in front of them and a school-issued social studies textbook stacked to one side. After reading silently for a few minutes, they pause at a paragraph where a bolded subheading states, "Majority approval does not guarantee that an action is right." The subject glances over at the social studies textbook, opens it to a bookmarked chapter on citizenship, and runs a finger down a page until they stop at a sentence that reads, "In a democracy, what most people agree on is usually what is right for society." They look back and forth between the two open pages, re-reading each line, then shift the philosophy book closer, tilt it toward the light, and continue reading the next few sentences that explain the claim with an example about an unfair law that many people support. After another short pause, they close the social studies textbook, leave the philosophy book open at the same page, and lean forward to keep reading without taking out any notebook or writing materials.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: Questions of Right and Wrong (chapter on majority approval and moral rightness)

episodes.observableAction: Late on a Saturday morning, the subject sits at the kitchen table with an open primary-school worksheet, pencil, and eraser, slowly copying addition problems while a cereal bowl and mug sit to one side as Caregiver B moves between the stove and sink rinsing dishes and checking a pot, then, after the subject pauses over a word problem and briefly raises a hand toward the hallway where a schoolbag lies before dropping it, Caregiver B comes over, pulls the worksheet closer, reads the problem aloud, takes the pencil, quickly writes the sums in the remaining blank spaces while saying the numbers, slides the worksheet back, tells the subject to put it in the schoolbag, and the subject carries the worksheet and pencil to the hallway, tucks the paper into the bag, and returns to the kitchen to place their empty bowl on the counter.

On a cool Saturday morning, the subject stands in the narrow kitchen pulling open and shutting the drawer where pencils and tape are usually kept, then crouches to look under the table and along the baseboard, glancing toward the hallway where a small backpack hangs on a hook; Caregiver B, rinsing a pan at the sink, asks what they are looking for, and when the subject says they cannot find their red-handled scissors for a school art project, Caregiver B wipes their hands on a towel, steps over, and together they check the table surface, the chair seats, and the floor, then move into the hallway to unzip the backpack and shake it lightly, pat the outside pockets, and look behind a shoe rack, until Caregiver B spots the scissors partly slid under a folded newspaper on the kitchen table, picks them up, holds them out, and the subject takes them and carries them back toward the backpack.

On a late Sunday afternoon, the subject sits at the kitchen table with an open exercise book, a sharpened pencil, and a math worksheet that has several subtraction problems partly filled in with uneven numbers and eraser smudges; Caregiver A comes in from the hallway carrying a work bag, sets it on a chair, glances at the worksheet, and, without asking anything, pulls the paper closer, takes the pencil from beside the subject’s hand, and quickly writes answers in the remaining blank spaces while standing over the table, pausing only to flip the page to check the next section before filling in those blanks as well. The subject watches, hands folded in their lap, as Caregiver A finishes the last problem, taps the pencil twice on the margin, pushes the worksheet and exercise book back toward the subject, and says that it is done now and should go straight into the schoolbag, then turns away to the sink and begins running water while the subject slides the worksheet into the exercise book, closes it, and carries the book out toward the hallway where their schoolbag hangs on a hook.

On a late Saturday morning, the subject sits at the kitchen table working on a colored drawing of a bus, buildings, and stick-figure people with pencils scattered around and a notebook titled "Community Places" open, while Caregiver B comes in carrying a folded shopping bag, looks at the drawing, points at the bus and asks if it is the stop near the market, then sets the bag on a chair, comments that the buildings look like the row under their flat while tapping near a drawn doorway, and finally reminds the subject to finish before lunch before moving to the sink as the subject continues coloring.

Late on a Saturday morning, the subject sits at the kitchen table with an open school notebook labeled "Our Family" and a worksheet asking for the year they moved into their flat, pencil poised over a blank line, while Caregiver A and Caregiver B, occupied with cooking and dishes, briefly disagree aloud about whether the move was in 2000 or 2001 before Caregiver B tells the subject to write "2001," and the subject writes it on the worksheet.

At the bus interchange beside the indoor market, the subject stands with Caregiver B near a route map while buses arrive and depart, listens as Caregiver B indicates the correct bus line and next departure, receives money and instructions to buy onions and soy sauce alone, walks into the market, navigates through shoppers to a produce stall to purchase onions using the list and coin purse, then goes to a nearby stall to select and pay for soy sauce, places the change and receipt in the coin purse, returns to the bus platforms carrying the bags, locates Caregiver B near the route sign, shows the remaining coins and receipt, and walks with Caregiver B to the marked waiting area for their bus.

On a warm Saturday afternoon in a classroom being used for an optional social studies workshop, the subject sits at a desk near the middle of the room while a history teacher stands by the whiteboard holding up a thin paperback titled "World Religions: An Introduction" and opens it to a marked page. The teacher reads aloud a short passage that defines the term "karma" as the idea that actions have consequences that shape future experiences, then writes the word and a brief paraphrase on the board. The subject follows along with a photocopied handout of the same page, tracing one sentence with a finger and glancing up as the teacher underlines the printed phrase "moral cause and effect" and asks the group to underline it on their copies. After a few minutes, the teacher closes the book, sets it on the front desk, and tells students they can borrow it from the school shelf or look for similar books at the branch library if they want to read more, while the subject slides the handout into a folder and watches as another student walks up to the desk to flip through the paperback.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: introductory explanation of karma in a world religions book

episodes.observableAction: On a quiet Saturday afternoon at the branch library, the subject sits alone at a study table near the shelves, with a school-issued history worksheet and a borrowed paperback titled "World Religions: An Introduction" open in front of them. After scanning the table of contents, the subject flips to the chapter on Eastern traditions, runs a finger down the page until finding the heading "Karma," and then reads a short section that describes karma as a kind of moral cause and effect that can influence future lives. The subject pauses to copy the word "karma" and a brief definition into the worksheet space labeled "Key Terms," looks back at the book to check the spelling of a phrase, writes it down, and then turns the page to glance at a diagram before closing the book halfway around a finger to hold their place and bending over the worksheet again to fill in another blank line.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: paperback survey book "World Religions: An Introduction"

episodes.observableAction: On a mild Saturday afternoon at the branch library, the subject stands in front of a waist-high shelf labeled "Non-Fiction" with several paperbacks and hardcovers lined up, tilts their head to read the spines of books on history, science, and religion, then pulls out a slim paperback titled "World Religions: An Introduction" and flips it open near the middle. After glancing at a nearby hardcover about world history and another book on philosophy without taking them off the shelf, the subject keeps the paperback in hand, walks to a nearby study table, and sits down. They open the book flat to a chapter heading, smooth the pages with one palm, and begin reading, occasionally pausing to look around the quiet room before returning their eyes to the text.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: World Religions: An Introduction (overview of major religious traditions)

episodes.observableAction: On a quiet Sunday afternoon at the branch library, the subject sits alone at a study table with a paperback copy of "World Religions: An Introduction" open beside a lined notebook and a ballpoint pen. After turning past the familiar chapter on Eastern traditions, the subject flips to a later chapter headed "Secular Worldviews" and pauses at a subsection titled "Atheism and Agnosticism." They read a paragraph that states, in bolded text, "It is possible to live a moral life without believing in any god or supernatural force," then glance up toward the nearby shelves where other religion titles stand before bending over the notebook. The subject writes the heading "Secular views" on one line, copies the sentence "moral life without believing in any god" underneath, and underlines the words "without believing." They then turn the page of the book to scan the next paragraph, tap the pen twice on the notebook margin, and continue copying a short definition into their notes while the low murmur of other patrons and the occasional beep from the circulation desk sound in the background.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: "World Religions: An Introduction" section on atheism and agnosticism

episode.observableAction: Late on a Saturday morning, the subject sits at the kitchen table with an open school notebook labeled "Our Family" and a worksheet asking for the year they moved into their flat, pencil poised over a blank line, while Caregiver A stands near the stove stirring a pan and Caregiver B dries dishes at the sink. The subject calls out to ask what year they moved here, and Caregiver A, without turning, says it was "two thousand," adding that the subject was in kindergarten then. Caregiver B looks over, frowns, and says no, it was "two thousand and one" because they remember carrying boxes up the stairs after New Year and the subject already having a school uniform. Caregiver A shakes their head and insists it was before that, mentioning a different job schedule, while Caregiver B repeats that it was the year of the New Year move and taps a dry plate on the counter for emphasis. The subject waits, pencil hovering, as the two caregivers briefly go back and forth about which school year it was and which cousin helped with the move, until Caregiver B finally tells the subject to write "2001" on the line, and the subject bends over the notebook and writes the numbers while both caregivers return to their tasks.

episode.observableAction: On a late Saturday morning at the bus interchange beside the indoor market, the subject stands with Caregiver B near a route map and timetable board, holding a folded shopping list and a small coin purse while buses pull in and out and other passengers move past. Caregiver B points to the posted schedule for the line that goes back toward their neighborhood, traces a finger down to the next departure time, and tells the subject that they will go into the market alone to buy onions and soy sauce while Caregiver B waits by the platform. After repeating the bus number and pointing toward the stall area entrance, Caregiver B hands the subject two bills and says to bring back the change and a receipt if there is one. The subject nods, tucks the money into the coin purse, walks through the sliding doors into the market, and weaves between shoppers and crates of vegetables until they reach a produce stall. They take the shopping list out, read from it, and ask the shopkeeper for a small bag of onions, then count coins and one bill into the shopkeeper’s hand, accept a plastic bag of onions and a few coins in change, and move on to a nearby stall with bottles and packets stacked on shelves. After scanning the labels, the subject picks up a bottle of soy sauce, shows it to the stallholder to confirm the price, pays with the remaining bill and some coins, and slips the change and a thin paper receipt back into the coin purse. Carrying the two bags, the subject walks back out to the bus platforms, looks along the row of waiting people until they spot Caregiver B near the route sign, and joins them. Caregiver B glances at the bags, asks if that is everything, and the subject opens the coin purse to show the remaining coins and folded receipt before both of them turn toward the marked waiting area for their bus.

episode.observableAction: On a warm Saturday afternoon in a classroom being used for an optional social studies workshop, the subject sits at a desk near the middle of the room while a history teacher stands by the whiteboard holding up a thin paperback titled "World Religions: An Introduction" and opens it to a marked page. The teacher reads aloud a short passage that defines the term "karma" as the idea that actions have consequences that shape future experiences, then writes the word and a brief paraphrase on the board. The subject follows along with a photocopied handout of the same page, tracing one sentence with a finger and glancing up as the teacher underlines the printed phrase "moral cause and effect" and asks the group to underline it on their copies. After a few minutes, the teacher closes the book, sets it on the front desk, and tells students they can borrow it from the school shelf or look for similar books at the branch library if they want to read more, while the subject slides the handout into a folder and watches as another student walks up to the desk to flip through the paperback.

episode.observableAction: On a quiet Saturday afternoon at the branch library, the subject sits alone at a study table near the shelves, with a school-issued history worksheet and a borrowed paperback titled "World Religions: An Introduction" open in front of them. After scanning the table of contents, the subject flips to the chapter on Eastern traditions, runs a finger down the page until finding the heading "Karma," and then reads a short section that describes karma as a kind of moral cause and effect that can influence future lives. The subject pauses to copy the word "karma" and a brief definition into the worksheet space labeled "Key Terms," looks back at the book to check the spelling of a phrase, writes it down, and then turns the page to glance at a diagram before closing the book halfway around a finger to hold their place and bending over the worksheet again to fill in another blank line.

episode.observableAction: On a quiet Sunday afternoon at the branch library, the subject sits alone at a study table with a paperback copy of "World Religions: An Introduction" open beside a lined notebook and a ballpoint pen. After turning past the familiar chapter on Eastern traditions, the subject flips to a later chapter headed "Secular Worldviews" and pauses at a subsection titled "Atheism and Agnosticism." They read a paragraph that states, in bolded text, "It is possible to live a moral life without believing in any god or supernatural force," then glance up toward the nearby shelves where other religion titles stand before bending over the notebook. The subject writes the heading "Secular views" on one line, copies the sentence "moral life without believing in any god" underneath, and underlines the words "without believing." They then turn the page of the book to scan the next paragraph, tap the pen twice on the notebook margin, and continue copying a short definition into their notes while the low murmur of other patrons and the occasional beep from the circulation desk sound in the background.

differencesFromE2V1: Household composition changes from one caregiver plus grandparent and younger sibling to two caregivers plus an older cousin.
Daily mobility changes from tram/bicycle emphasis to bus/walking with occasional rides from relatives.
The public-space mix changes from community workshop, tram loop and river fields to branch library/civic hall, bus-market interchange and canalside park.

The calendar shifts later while preserving the same ordinary childhood-through-adolescence age span and urban public-institution access pattern.
worldAuthoringRecord.reasonForDifferences: Create a second ordinary, source-free developmental substrate that is materially distinct from E2-V1 while preserving comparable access constraints. The changes were not selected to target any known remembered/not_remembered episode, desired adult identity, target personality, genome signal, or N2 score.
worldAuthoringRecord.knownConfoundDisclosure: The author could not unsee E2-V1 or the failed N1-on-A0 run. This record makes that author-after-observation fact explicit; N2 therefore remains development evidence rather than an independent population sample.
